data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":{"adopted_commitment_refs":[],"disanalogies":["Biological evolution lacks the intentional choice element present in scientific theory selection.","Natural selection operates on reproductive fitness, whereas corroboration operates on informational content and test severity.","Evolutionary success is retrospective, while scientific preference is prospective (aimed at future tests)."],"overturn_conditions":["If a less corroborated theory consistently outperforms a highly corroborated one in new domains without being falsified, the procedural rule loses its normative force.","If the concept of 'severity' of a test cannot be defined independently of the theory being tested, the entire mechanism becomes circular."],"shared_structure":["Selection based on survival of severe trials rather than probability accumulation.","Distinction between pragmatic utility for action and logical justification of truth.","Reliance on a metaphysical axiom (regularity of nature) to bridge the gap between test results and future action."],"source_memory_refs":["SRC_003","SRC_007"],"transfer_claims":["Just as organisms surviving harsh environments are not 'more probable' to survive future changes but are the only viable candidates for further adaptation, corroborated theories are the only viable candidates for further scientific progress.","The 'fitness' of a theory is its ability to withstand falsification, not its statistical likelihood of being true."]},"claim":"Popper's preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on his own terms not as an inductive inference that the theory is more likely true, but as a procedural rule of critical rationalism: we prefer the theory that has withstood the most severe tests because it offers the best available target for future falsification, thereby maximizing the growth of knowledge. This preference does not smuggle in induction because it makes no probabilistic claim about the future; it simply acknowledges that a theory surviving severe tests has higher 'verisimilitude' (truth-likeness) relative to a refuted one, even if verisimilitude cannot be quantitatively measured. The cost of accepting this view is the abandonment of the hope for a formal, algorithmic method to determine which theory is 'best' in a final sense, leaving scientists with a fallible, metaphysical faith in the regularity of nature to justify acting on the best-tested theory.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If verisimilitude is proven formally incoherent within Popper's framework (as argued by Miller and Tich\u00fd), then the defense collapses unless a non-quantitative notion of 'closeness to truth' can be salvaged.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the preference for corroborated theories implicitly assumes that the future will resemble the past (uniformity of nature) without explicitly stating it as a metaphysical postulate, then induction has been smuggled back in.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If Popper's distinction between the 'logic of discovery' and the 'context of action' fails to provide a normative reason for preferring one theory over another, then the preference is merely psychological, not rational.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Critical Rationalism Procedural Rule","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
